gap: No result ChatGPT got states that EcoFlow's '1,200 W' STREAM Ultra feeds only 800 W into the outlet on its own, and needs the separate STREAM Microinverter to reach the 1,200 W cap set by Utah and Maryland. Its two AC outlets also give only 800 W in an outage, against 1,800 W continuous from a BLUETTI AC180.
standout_why: ChatGPT's saved chat lists no search results. Its answer showed an 'EcoFlow STREAM' catalog card with no output, cycle-life or certification figures. The top organic results for the query (pv-magazine guidebook, WRI, TechRadar, EcoFlow's own 'Where Is Plug-In Solar Legal' tracker dated 2026-07-04) cover state wattage caps (1,200 W in Utah, Maryland, Maine, Virginia and New York if signed; 1,920 W in Colorado). They do not separate a product's grid feed-in watts from its outlet watts or its solar input watts. EcoFlow's tracker names STREAM Ultra as available in Utah and Maryland but gives no output limit. Our current page writes 'Up to 1,200 W with microinverter' in the solar column and lists 1.92 kWh with no cycle basis. The 800 W standalone figure and the 800 W outlet ceiling are new. The cycle-life basis difference is new too, but I only have half of it sourced (see unsourced).
decides: This confirms the split in the pick rather than flipping it. For cutting the bill in Utah or Maryland, STREAM Ultra is the only plug-in battery here with UL 1741 and IEEE 1547. But one unit only feeds 800 W, so a renter needs the microinverter bundle to use the full 1,200 W the law allows, and the price should be quoted for that bundle. For outage backup, STREAM Ultra's 800 W outlet ceiling loses to a power station kit: the AC180 gives 1,800 W continuous and a 2,700 W surge, works in every state and needs no grid tie. Cycle claims are not comparable at face value. EcoFlow quotes 6,000 cycles with no end-point on its US page and 'to 70%' on its UK spec page. BLUETTI states its cycles to 80%.
